# Chart names, translated

gog has no chart-type atoms: a histogram is a sentence, not a word. But people
look for plots by name, so this appendix is the index of names. It is the one
place organized by chart name. The [cookbook](cookbook/one-variable.qmd) covers
the same plots organized by question, which is usually the better place to
start.

Column names here are placeholders. Replace them with your own.

## Names with a one-line answer

Each of these names is one gog sentence. The left column is the name you
know, and the right column is the sentence that draws it. Where a name needs
a second word, it follows the sentence in the same cell.

| The name you know | The sentence |
|---|---|
| Scatter plot | `point + x(a) + y(b)` |
| Bubble chart | `point + x(a) + y(b) + size(c)` |
| Strip plot | `point + x(category) + y(measure)`, or swap the axes to draw it sideways |
| Bar chart | `bar + x(category) + y(measure)` |
| Horizontal bar chart | `bar + x(measure) + y(category)` |
| Hatched (print-safe) bars | `bar + x(category) + y(measure) + style(pattern = "hatch")`, also `"crosshatch"`/`"stripes"`/`"grid"`/`"dots"` |
| Count (frequency) chart | `bar * count + x(category)` |
| Proportion chart | `bar * proportion + x(category)` |
| Histogram | `bar * bin + x(measure)`; `bin(30)` sets the number of bins and `bin(width = 5)` sets their width |
| Frequency polygon | `line * bin + x(measure)` |
| Outline (step) histogram | `step * bin + x(measure)` |
| Overlaid histograms | `bar * bin + x(measure) + color(group)` |
| Density plot | `line * density + x(measure)` |
| Line chart / time series | `line + x(time) + y(measure)` |
| Multi-series lines by dash (no color) | `line + x(time) + y(measure) + pattern(series)`, add `color(series)` for redundant encoding |
| Step chart | `step + x(a) + y(b)` |
| Empirical CDF | `step` over cumulative shares, worked example in [Step](marks/step.qmd) |
| Area chart | `area + x(a) + y(b)` |
| Spread / range band | `ribbon * range + x(a) + y(b)`, split by group with `color(group)` |
| Confidence band (computed) | `ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(a) + y(b)`, often under a `line * mean` trend |
| Confidence band (pre-computed) | `ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a)`, bounds you already have (a model's standard error, a standard error of measurement) |
| Unfilled (dashed) error band | `line * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a) + style(pattern = "dashed")`, the upper and lower edges drawn as two lines, with nothing filled between them |
| Min–max envelope, as two lines | `line * range + x(a) + y(b)`, the unfilled counterpart to `ribbon * range` |
| Dashed / dotted line | any `line`/`step` `+ style(pattern = "dashed")` (or `"dotted"`) |
| Trend line / smoother / LOESS | `line * smooth + x(a) + y(b)` |
| Summary bars (mean per group) | `bar * mean + x(category) + y(measure)`, also `sum`, `median`, `max`, `min` |
| Grouped bars (side by side) | `bar * mean * dodge + x(category) + y(measure) + color(group)`, where `* dodge` gives each group its own bar side by side inside the category's slot |
| Colorblind-safe grouped bars | add `+ pattern(group)` to the grouped bars: one column drives both the color and the hatch, so the two share one merged legend |
| Ranked bars | add `+ order(measure, desc = TRUE)` |
| Small multiples / trellis / conditioning plot / facets | `plot \| facet(category)`, `plot / facet(category)`, or both for a grid |
| Small multiples of 3-D plots | any cube sentence `\| facet(category)`: each panel holds its own cube, all drawn from the same angle |
| 3-D scatter | `point + x(a) + y(b) + z(c)`, view angle via `space(turn = , tilt = )` |
| 3-D trajectory / space curve | `path + x(a) + y(b) + z(c)`, the rows joined in table order, in the cube |
| Surface plot / wireframe | `surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c)` over a table with one row per (x, y) crossing, every `a` value paired with every `b` value; `style(border_color = "white")` draws the mesh lines, `color(c)` shades it by height |
| Terrain / elevation / bathymetry | the same sentence: a height over a plane is a `surface`, whatever the height means |
| Response surface | `surface + x(factor1) + y(factor2) + z(response)` over the design grid; from a fitted model, predict onto a grid first and name that table in the sentence |
| 3-D density surface | `surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space()`, the estimate raised as height. That is the third geometry of one field, which `zone * density` paints and `path * density` traces |
| Profile plot (categories joined) | `line * mean + x(category) + y(measure)`, one summary per category with the path across them; `step` stays flat between categories instead of sloping |
| Filled profile | `area * mean + x(category) + y(measure)`, the same boundary filled to the baseline |
| Connected scatterplot | `path + x(a) + y(b)`, the rows joined in the table's order rather than sorted by x; `style(arrow = "end")` says which end is last |
| Trajectory / route / hysteresis loop | the same sentence: any reading whose *order* is the data's is `path`, not `line` |
| Annotation arrow / callout | `data(two_rows) + path + style(arrow = "end")`, layered over the plot; the note itself is `data(one_row) + text + label(note)` |
| Rose / coxcomb / wind rose | `bar * count + x(direction) + polar()`, the bar chart read in a circle |
| Radar / spider plot | `line * mean + x(category) + y(measure) + polar()`, the profile bent into a circle; `area` fills it |
| Pie chart | `bar * count * stack + color(category) + polar()`, a stacked bar in polar coordinates; the category is a *split*, not a position |
| Sunburst | `zone * partition(a, b, c) + x(measure) + polar()`, worked example in [Polar](polar.qmd). One ring per level of a tree, each arc as wide as its share. The hierarchy is **columns**, outermost first. A blank level ends that branch early, so the branch stops short of the outer ring. That is what makes the rim ragged. `y(depth, limits = c(0, n))` puts the hole in the middle, and `text * partition(…) + label(name)` names the nodes, reading the same centers the zone computed |
| Icicle / partition chart | the sunburst's sentence with `polar()` taken off, which is the whole difference: depth up the y axis, share across the x. The two names are one coordinate space apart, exactly as a rose and a bar chart are, or a pie and a stacked bar |
| Treemap | `bar * sum + y(value) + color(category) + nest()`, the same shares carried by area rather than by angle ([Nest](nest.qmd)) |
| Nested treemap | the same, plus `x(group)`: one region per group, its rows packed inside |
| Labeled treemap | the same, plus a `text` layer: `+ text + label(name)` writes each region's name at its center, which is what a packing needs once the split has too many levels for a legend. A name wider than its own region is left out, and the plot reports how many names it dropped ([Nest](nest.qmd)) |
| Pie of a measure | `bar * sum * stack + y(amount) + color(category) + polar()`, also `proportion` for shares on the axis |
| Share-of-total column | the same sentence without `polar()`, one segmented bar |
| Polar histogram | `bar * bin + x(bearing) + polar()`, bins as wedges of a measured angle |
| Circular (cyclical) line | `line + x(hour) + y(measure) + polar()`, both ends of the cycle in the data |
| Polar scatter | `point + x(bearing) + y(measure) + polar()` |
| Contour plot / density contours | `path * density + x(a) + y(b)`, the contours of a density estimated over the plane; `density(levels = )` says how many, `group(category)` estimates one field per group. `zone * density(levels = )` fills one band per level, on the levels the contours trace. The filled reading draws one field wrongly: a **crater**, which is a ring-shaped cluster with a hollow middle. A band around a hollow is a shape with a hole, and gog has no mark for one |
| 2-D density heatmap | `zone * density + x(a) + y(b)`, the same field painted as cells instead of traced as lines |
| Filled contour / filled density | `zone * density(levels = 8) + x(a) + y(b)`, eight bands, one per level; the same `levels` a `path` traces |
| Binned heatmap | `zone * bin + x(a) + y(b)`, cells colored by how many rows fell in each |
| Hexbin | `zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(a) + y(b)`, a staggered mesh, whose cells form no straight rows or columns for a reader to mistake for structure in the data |
| Heat strip / binned distribution per group | `zone * bin + x(number) + y(category)`, the mixed mesh: the continuous axis cut into cells, one row of cells per category. Every row is cut on the same edges, so the cells line up down the plot |
| Choropleth | `zone` with `group(country)` and `map()`: `group` says which rows belong to one region, and the region's own boundary becomes the zone's sides ([Map](map.qmd)) |
| Candlestick / OHLC chart | two layers over one table, worked example in [Zone](marks/zone.qmd): `interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir)` is the whisker and `zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1)` the body, over `x(session)`. Four numbers a session, and no new channel for them. `bounds` reads a low value and a high value, and a rectangle's bottom and top are the same two numbers. The `opacity` and the named sides both replace a zone default meant for highlighting: here the rectangle *is* the data |
| Waterfall / bridge chart | `zone * bounds(base, top, start = left, end = right) + x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1)`, worked example in [Zone](marks/zone.qmd). `stack` accumulates *within* a position and a waterfall accumulates *across* positions, so the running total is arithmetic that belongs with the data, in the host language. The subtotal bars start at 0. `left` and `right` sit just inside each slot's edges, which is what leaves a gap between the bars |
| Funnel chart | `zone * bounds(lo, hi) + y(stage) + style(opacity = 1)`, worked example in [Zone](marks/zone.qmd), with `text + label(n) + x(mid)` for the numbers inside. The columns `lo` and `hi` hold `-n/2` and `n/2`, computed in the host, which is the same arithmetic the waterfall uses for its running total. A funnel is a bar chart whose blocks are centered on zero. Centering is arithmetic on two columns, so a funnel is not a chart type. The measure goes on `x` because `y(stage)` is a category. Nothing in the sentence has to ask for that, because the kinds of the columns settle it. gog draws no sloped connectors between the stages, on purpose. A connector spans the gap between two categories. That gap carries no values, so no scale can give its width a meaning |

## Names that need more

These names need a paragraph rather than a line. All but one of them draw, and
the entry gives the sentence. Where one does not, the entry says so first, and
then says what the closest sentence leaves out.

| The name | The sentence, and what to know |
|---|---|
| Box plot | `box + x(group) + y(value)`, the five-number summary per group |
| Violin plot | `ribbon * density + x(group) + y(value)`, the shape the box plot's five numbers summarize. `density(compare = )` says whether the widths carry each group's row count (the default) or draw every violin to the same area |
| Half violin | `area * density + x(group) + y(value)`: the same estimate, closed on the slot's center line instead of on its own mirror image. That is what separates `area` from `ribbon` everywhere in the book |
| Ridgeline plot / joyplot | `area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(value) + y(group)`, the half violin with its axes exchanged, one density per category, each on its own line, sharing one measure axis. `reach` is in **slots**, so past `0.5` the ridges leave their own slots, which is what makes a joyplot. To outline it, add a layer: `line * density + style(color = "black")` reads the same estimate and traces the top of the fill |
| Jittered strip plot | `point * jitter + x(group) + y(value)`, the `jitter` collision modifier spreads coincident points along the category axis |
| Labeled scatter, names not overlapping | `point + text * repel + x(a) + y(b) + label(name)`, where the `repel` collision modifier moves each word off the other words and off the dots. When a label has moved far, `repel` draws a thin line back to its point |
| Stacked bars / areas | `bar * sum * stack` / `area * sum * stack` with a `color` split, the `stack` collision modifier (grouped bars are its sibling `dodge`) |
| 100% stacked bar / filled area | `bar * count * stack(share = TRUE) + x(a) + color(b)`, every pile is divided by its own slot's total. Each pile then reaches 1, so the plot shows composition and no longer shows size. Any measurement fills the same way, `sum` included |
| Streamgraph | `area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(t) + y(v) + color(g)`, worked example in [Transforms](transforms.qmd). The foot of each pile is placed to keep the bands as flat as possible, so a band's shape is its own rather than the sum of everything below it. `share` and `baseline` are the pile's two independent choices, and you can use them together |
| ThemeRiver | `area * stack(baseline = "center")`, the same sentence with the *symmetric* layout instead [@havre2000]. Often confused with the streamgraph and not the same plot: this one centers every pile, and the streamgraph keeps its bands as flat as possible. The streamgraph's designers argue that readers compare values more accurately on it [@byron2008] |
| Alluvial diagram | `ribbon * flow(a, b, c) + y(count)`, with `zone * flow(...)` for the stage slots and `text * flow(...) + label(name)` for their names, worked example in [Flow](flow.qmd). One row of the table is one path through the stages. Between each pair of neighboring stages, one band carries that path's size |
| Sankey diagram | Not drawn in the general form. The alluvial draws the same merged bands. Reduce the table to one pair of stages at a time, and each band is the flow between that pair. The general many-source form, given as a list of nodes and a list of links, is a different input shape and is not read ([Flow](flow.qmd) says where the limits are) |
| Network diagram / node-link graph | `edge * layout(from, to) + network()`, with `point * layout(...)` for the nodes, `size(degree)` sizing each node by its relations, and `text * layout(...) + label(name)` for their names, worked example in [Network](network.qmd). The engine computes every position, so the picture is the same in all four languages. State an angle, `network(turn = 35, tilt = 20)`, and the same layout becomes a cube the reader can drag in the web edition |
| Relative-frequency histogram | `bar * bin * proportion + x(number)`, the histogram's own counts read as fractions of n, on the mesh `bar * bin` cuts |
| Heatmap | A heatmap is drawn on two continuous axes, on two categorical axes, or on one of each. The transform you need depends on which kinds you have. A *continuous* axis needs cutting, so `zone * bin` counts the rows per cell: both axes for the classic heatmap, one for the mixed mesh. A *categorical* axis arrives cut, so on two of them `zone * count` tallies into the slots, and `zone + color(value)` draws a table you already have. `zone * density` is the third route, and it estimates a value at each cell of a plane rather than counting rows |
| Summary heatmap / matrix of means | `zone * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(column)` reduces the named column within every cell two categories cross, and `sum`/`median`/`max`/`min` read the same mesh. The column is named on `color` because that is the channel a zone measures with. A summary reduces in place, so the channel that names the column also receives the result, exactly as `y` does on `bar * mean + x + y` |
| Tile plot / calendar heatmap | `zone + x(a) + y(b) + color(value)`, one cell per pair of categories, filling the slot each one owns |
| Confusion matrix | `zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted)` tallies the raw rows; `zone * proportion` reads them as shares of the whole. Normalizing per *true class*, a share within each row of the grid, is not one of these: `stack(share = )` divides a pile by its slot's total, and a grid has no pile to divide |
| Correlation matrix / corrplot | Drawn as a tile plot, once the correlations are a table. Compute them where your data lives, then reshape the result so that each row holds one pair of variables and their correlation. `zone + x(var1) + y(var2) + color(r)` draws that table. gog computes no correlations, and that is the host language's job. A channel names a column; it does not compute one |
| Donut chart | `zone * partition(category) + x(measure) + y(depth, limits = c(0, 2)) + polar()`, worked example in [Polar](polar.qmd). A donut is a [sunburst](polar.qmd) of a tree one level deep. The hole is not a shape that gog draws. It is a stretch of the radial axis with nothing standing on it, which is what the stated `limits` leave empty. The plain *pie* (`bar * count * stack`) is the one reading that cannot ask for a hole. It measures with the angle, so its radius is a constant and has no domain to widen. That is a fact about the reading rather than a gap, so there is no `polar(hole = )` and no plan for one |
| Animated (time-lapse) chart | any sentence `+ play(year)`: faceting read in time |
| Marginal / joint plot (scatter with histograms in its margins) | <code>top / (main &#124; right)</code>: three ordinary plots and the two composition operators. There is no chart type and no `ggMarginal()`. The marginals align and share their scale because both name the same column on the same axis. That shared scale is the one thing composition adds ([Composition](composition.qmd)). Any mark can be the marginal: a histogram, a box, a violin, a dot plot |
| Dendrogram / cluster tree | `path * cluster(value, over = profile) + x(item)` joins the closest leaves one pair at a time, and each join's distance goes on an axis of its own. `item` is the column that names the leaves, and binding it to `y` instead lays the tree on its side ([Cluster](cluster.qmd)). *Dendrogram* is Greek for tree drawing, which is what *cluster tree* says in English |
| Clustered heatmap | `zone * cluster(over = profile)` reorders a tile plot's slots into the tree's leaf order. The full figure is the marginal plot, with one tree over the tiles and one beside them, and each shared axis takes its tree's order ([Cluster](cluster.qmd#the-clustered-heatmap)) |
| 3-D surface | The same sentence as **Surface plot / wireframe** in the first table, `surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c)` over a grid table, or `surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space()` to raise an estimated field. A *scatter* cannot be one. It is refused toward `point` rather than drawn as an empty sheet, because a surface's faces span the gaps between its samples. A surface needs its samples on a grid |
| Terraced / stepped surface (one value per cell) | `surface * bin * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v)` cuts the floor into cells and lays a flat plateau on each, with a vertical face at every step. This is the sentence for a design that measures one number per condition. An interpolated sheet would claim a gradient nobody observed ([Surface](marks/surface.qmd)) |

If the name you are looking for is in neither table, it is usually one of the
listed plots drawn with different settings. Ask what question the chart answers,
and start from the [cookbook](cookbook/one-variable.qmd). If the name is one of
ggplot2's function names, [Coverage](coverage.qmd) lists the same plots, indexed
that way. It sorts each name into four: refused, the host language's job,
missing with the direction settled, and not decided either way.
